difficultyReason: The flaw is a necessary/sufficient confusion embedded in a medical context. All five answer choices are dense mini-arguments; two plausible traps replicate the surface vocabulary without matching the directional swap. Students who misidentify the flaw as base-rate reversal will select a wrong answer.
stimulus: Dr. Alvarez argues that anyone who has Rennick syndrome will test positive on the Halpern screening. Marcus tested positive on the Halpern screening. Therefore, Marcus probably has Rennick syndrome.
questionStem: The flawed reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to the flawed reasoning in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Anyone who completes the advanced licensing exam is qualified to practice independently. Yolanda is qualified to practice independently. Therefore, Yolanda probably completed the advanced licensing exam.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Anyone who studies abroad for at least one semester will become fluent in the local language. Priya studied abroad for one semester. Therefore, Priya is probably fluent in the local language.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most people who score highly on the aptitude test go on to excel in engineering. Tomás excels in engineering. Therefore, Tomás probably scored highly on the aptitude test.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Anyone who receives the merit scholarship must have an outstanding academic record. Devon has an outstanding academic record. Therefore, Devon will probably receive the merit scholarship.

choices.label: E
choices.text: No one who has completed the detoxification protocol will test positive for trace compounds. Simone has not completed the protocol. Therefore, Simone will probably test positive for trace compounds.

explanations.correct: Stimulus structure: If Rennick syndrome → positive test (sufficient condition). Marcus has positive test → therefore Marcus has Rennick syndrome. This treats a sufficient condition as if it were also necessary — affirming the consequent. Answer A replicates this exactly: If complete advanced exam → qualified (sufficient). Yolanda is qualified → therefore she completed the exam. Same affirming-the-consequent flaw at matching probabilistic strength.
explanations.A: Correct. If completing the exam is sufficient for qualification, being qualified does not entail completing the exam — other routes to qualification may exist. The argument affirms the consequent, exactly as the stimulus does.
explanations.B: This is a valid modus ponens inference: the premise establishes a sufficient condition (study abroad → fluent), and the conclusion follows by applying that condition to Priya. No flaw — trap for students who focus only on surface conditionals without checking validity.
explanations.C: This commits base-rate reversal ('most X have Y; this thing has Y; so it's probably an X'), not affirming the consequent. The stimulus's premise is a universal conditional, not a 'most' statement. Different flaw family.
explanations.D: This confuses necessary with sufficient in the opposite direction: the stimulus affirms the consequent, but D draws a conclusion about obtaining a sufficient cause from possessing what is only a necessary precondition — treating a necessary condition as sufficient. The directional error is different from the stimulus's.
explanations.E: This denies the antecedent: 'If completed protocol → not positive; Simone has not completed protocol → Simone will probably test positive.' Related conditional fallacy, but structurally distinct from affirming the consequent.

difficultyReason: The stimulus commits a composition fallacy — inferring a property of the whole from properties of the parts. All five answer choices are dense mini-arguments in varied domains; one answer commits a valid inference from an analogous structure, one commits division (the inverse fallacy), and one is a different quantifier error. Students who misidentify the flaw will be lured by the division-fallacy trap.
stimulus: Every section of Hargrove's new economic policy proposal has been praised by independent analysts as carefully reasoned and internally consistent. Therefore, the proposal as a whole is almost certainly carefully reasoned and internally consistent.
questionStem: Which one of the following arguments exhibits flawed reasoning most similar to that exhibited by the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Each chapter of Delacroix's biography of Empress Theodora is historically accurate and meticulously sourced. Therefore, the biography as a whole is almost certainly historically accurate and meticulously sourced.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Rowan's symphony is widely regarded as a masterpiece of modern composition. Therefore, each movement of the symphony is almost certainly a masterpiece in its own right.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Every ingredient in Chef Marconi's signature dish has been certified as organic and locally sourced. Therefore, Chef Marconi's restaurant probably uses only organic and locally sourced ingredients in all its dishes.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Most of the essays in the anthology were written by established scholars. Therefore, the anthology as a whole was probably written by established scholars.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Each member of the investigative panel has demonstrated expertise in financial regulation. Therefore, the panel as a whole almost certainly has the expertise needed to conduct the investigation.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: every part (section) has property P → the whole (proposal) has property P. This is the fallacy of composition — properties of parts do not automatically transfer to the whole, because section-level coherence doesn't guarantee cross-section coherence. Answer A mirrors this exactly: every part (chapter) has property P (accurate, sourced) → the whole (biography) has property P. A biography could have inaccuracies or inconsistencies arising from how chapters relate to one another, even if each chapter is internally accurate.
explanations.A: Correct. Replicates the composition fallacy: part-level property (accurate chapter) → whole-level property (accurate biography). The whole can fail to be accurate even when each part is, due to contradictions or gaps between chapters.
explanations.B: This commits the fallacy of division — inferring a property of the parts from a property of the whole. That is the inverse of the composition fallacy in the stimulus. Close structural relative but a different error.
explanations.C: This is a scope expansion error — from a property of one dish to a property of the entire restaurant's menu. Not composition (part→whole) but rather generalization from one instance to a broader class. Different flaw.
explanations.D: This uses the quantifier 'most' rather than 'every/each,' and the inference is from a statistical majority among parts to a property of the whole. This is a weaker version of the error, but the premise is probabilistic rather than universal, making the flaw structurally distinct.
explanations.E: This is a valid inference. Panel-level expertise in a domain is constituted by the expertise of its members; when each member has the relevant expertise, the collective body plausibly has that expertise. No flaw — trap for students who assume any part→whole inference is flawed.

difficultyReason: The stimulus commits base-rate reversal in a linguistics/history context: 'Most X's have property Y; this thing has property Y; therefore it is probably an X.' Each answer choice is a dense five-line mini-argument. One trap commits the same quantifier move but reverses direction; one is a valid base-rate inference; one changes absolute vs. proportional framing. Students must track quantifier direction precisely.
stimulus: Most ancient inscriptions that originated in the Keldaran trading network were written on fired clay tablets. The newly excavated inscription at Mervasa was written on a fired clay tablet. Therefore, the Mervasa inscription was probably produced within the Keldaran trading network.
questionStem: Which one of the following contains a pattern of flawed reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Most prize-winning wines from the Corenne valley are aged in French oak barrels. The Domaine Pelletier reserve is aged in French oak barrels. Therefore, the Domaine Pelletier reserve is probably a prize-winning wine from the Corenne valley.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Most manuscripts produced in the Aldric scriptorium were written on vellum. The Aldric scriptorium produced the Hartwell Psalter. Therefore, the Hartwell Psalter was probably written on vellum.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The majority of architectural features found in Velmorian temples also appear in Dassine civic buildings. The Harwell colonnade contains several features found in Dassine civic buildings. Therefore, the Harwell colonnade was probably built by Velmorian craftsmen.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Most structural engineers who specialize in seismic retrofitting have completed graduate-level coursework in geotechnical analysis. Petra has completed such coursework. Therefore, Petra is probably a structural engineer who specializes in seismic retrofitting.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The Sorvaine Bridge was constructed using techniques documented in most Fenwick-era engineering manuals. Most bridges built using those techniques have remained structurally sound for over two centuries. Therefore, the Sorvaine Bridge has probably remained structurally sound for over two centuries.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: Most [category] have [property Y]; this item has [property Y]; therefore this item is probably [category]. This is base-rate reversal — the frequency of Y within the Keldaran network tells us nothing about the frequency of Keldaran-origin among all Y-bearing objects; other networks may also use fired clay. Answer A replicates this exactly: Most prize-winning Corenne wines have [property Y = French oak]; Domaine Pelletier has [property Y]; therefore it is probably a prize-winning Corenne wine. Many non-prize-winning or non-Corenne wines are also aged in French oak, so the inference reverses the base rate.
explanations.A: Correct. Mirrors the stimulus's base-rate reversal: most members of category X have property Y → item with Y is probably in category X. Ignores that property Y may be widespread outside category X.
explanations.B: This is a valid inference. The premise states most items produced by a specific source have property Y, and the conclusion is that a known product of that source probably has Y. Modus ponens from base rate — no flaw. Trap for students who focus on the 'most … therefore probably' surface structure without checking inferential direction.
explanations.C: The argument involves an additional inferential step (shared features imply shared craftsmen) that introduces a causal attribution error — not base-rate reversal. The property in question (Dassine civic features) is shared across both Velmorian and Dassine contexts, but the flaw is misattributing causation rather than reversing a base rate.
explanations.D: This commits base-rate reversal using a universal-ish 'most … have completed coursework' → 'Petra has coursework → Petra is probably in the specialization.' Structurally close, but notice the subject and predicate are reversed relative to the stimulus in a different way: in the stimulus the category is a geographic-cultural network; here the category is a professional specialization defined partly by the very credential cited, making the flaw slightly different in kind. More importantly, this answer is a strong trap — students should recognize that answer A more cleanly replicates the stimulus because the property (French oak aging) is widely shared outside the target category, exactly as fired clay tablets were shared outside the Keldaran network.
explanations.E: This chains two 'most' premises toward a conclusion about a specific item — a different quantifier-chain structure. The first premise links the bridge to a technique; the second links the technique to longevity. Neither premise reverses a base rate; the argument's flaw (if any) is in how two probabilistic premises combine, not in reversing part-to-whole frequency.
